title: Recurrent Miscarriage - History, Differentials and Investigations
patient_instructions: You are Sophie Nguyen, a 33-year-old teacher, presenting to a GP because you have had three miscarriages, all in the first trimester (around 8-10 weeks), over the past two years. You and your partner have been trying to have a baby and you feel devastated and anxious. Your periods are regular. You have never carried a pregnancy past the first trimester. You have never had products of conception tested. You have no known thyroid, diabetes or clotting problems, but you sometimes feel the cold more than others (do not volunteer this unless asked about temperature preference). No joint pains or rashes. No previous uterine surgery or terminations. You have a cat at home. You smoke about 5 cigarettes a day and drink 3-4 coffees daily and occasional wine. Your partner is supportive. You are up to date with cervical screening. If asked about your fears, you say: 'I just want to know why this keeps happening and whether I can ever have a healthy baby.' Affect: tearful when discussing the losses, but cooperative. Only volunteer emotional distress and the cat/smoking/caffeine details when specifically asked.
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice. Sophie Nguyen, a 33-year-old woman, has had three first-trimester miscarriages and attends to find out why and what can be done. In the next 8 minutes: take a focused, empathetic history; outline to the patient the likely groups of causes; and explain which investigations you would arrange. You do not need to examine the patient.
examiner_instructions: Look for an empathetic, structured history that acknowledges grief early. Reward exploration of the losses (number, gestation, any POC testing), pregnancy/surgical history, menstrual history and targeted screening across the differential groups (uterine, endocrine, immunological, genetic, environmental). Strong candidates state a correct definition (miscarriage = loss before 20 weeks in Australia; recurrent = two or more per ESHRE or three or more consecutive per RCOG/RANZCOG) and name an evidence-based work-up (parental karyotype +/- POC cytogenetics, pelvic ultrasound +/- hysteroscopy/HSG, antiphospholipid antibodies repeated 12 weeks apart, TSH/thyroid antibodies, diabetes screen). They should NOT order routine TORCH serology or serum progesterone, and should name antiphospholipid syndrome as the key treatable cause (aspirin + LMWH in pregnancy). Prompt if needed: 'Which single genetic test is the classic must-not-forget on the investigation card?' (parental karyotype).

criteria: Acknowledges grief and emotional impact early and sensitively
Explores the miscarriages: number, gestation at each loss, any testing of products of conception
Takes pregnancy/surgical, menstrual and family history
Screens differential groups: endocrine (thyroid/PCOS/diabetes/prolactin), immunological (clots, joint pain, rashes), environmental (smoking, alcohol, caffeine, stress)
States correct Australian definitions (loss before 20 weeks; recurrent = 2+ ESHRE or 3+ consecutive RCOG/RANZCOG)
Groups differentials logically: uterine, endocrine, immunological/thrombophilic, genetic, environmental
Identifies antiphospholipid syndrome as the most important treatable cause
Names evidence-based work-up: parental karyotype +/- POC cytogenetics, pelvic ultrasound +/- hysteroscopy/HSG
Requests antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant + anticardiolipin, repeated 12 weeks apart), TSH/thyroid antibodies and diabetes testing

Avoids non-recommended tests (routine TORCH, serum progesterone) and offers preconception advice (folic acid, smoking/caffeine reduction) and referral to a recurrent-miscarriage/early-pregnancy clinic
Empathic, uses supportive language and checks understanding
Instils realistic hope and offers early-pregnancy reassurance scanning/counselling in the next pregnancy

red_flags: Antiphospholipid syndrome - the key treatable cause; if missed, recurrent loss and thrombotic risk continue
Second-trimester or late losses suggesting cervical insufficiency or a uterine anomaly requiring specialist assessment
Signs of a treatable endocrinopathy (uncontrolled thyroid disease or diabetes) that increase miscarriage risk
Significant psychological distress/grief requiring active support and follow-up
australian_guidelines: RANZCOG: recurrent miscarriage investigation includes parental karyotype +/- products-of-conception cytogenetics, pelvic ultrasound (+/- hysteroscopy/HSG), antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin repeated 12 weeks apart), TSH/thyroid antibodies and diabetes screening; routine TORCH serology is not recommended
Antiphospholipid syndrome in pregnancy is managed with low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic heparin (LMWH)
RACGP preconception care: folic acid supplementation, rubella/varicella serology, optimisation of thyroid function, glycaemic control and BMI, and smoking/alcohol/caffeine reduction
Australian terminology: miscarriage is pregnancy loss before 20 weeks' gestation (not 24 weeks)
learning_objectives: Define miscarriage and recurrent miscarriage using current Australian/international thresholds
Construct a grouped differential and evidence-based investigation plan for recurrent pregnancy loss
Identify antiphospholipid syndrome and its pregnancy management
Deliver emotionally sensitive counselling and appropriate referral for recurrent pregnancy loss
key_points: Parental karyotype is the classic must-not-forget investigation on the AMC recall card
A stem of 'trying for pregnancy for years' may be recurrent miscarriage rather than infertility
Antiphospholipid antibody testing must be repeated 12 weeks apart to confirm the diagnosis
Vaginal micronised progesterone may be offered for women with recurrent miscarriage and early-pregnancy bleeding

citations.claim: Endocrine contributors including hypothyroidism, PCOS and hyperprolactinaemia feature in the diagnostic reasoning for menstrual/weight disturbance, supporting endocrine screening and TSH/prolactin investigation.
Thyroid disease, SLE and other endocrine disorders are recognised causes underlying abnormal reproductive/menstrual patterns, supporting thyroid and immunological (SLE/antiphospholipid) screening.
Uterine structural pathology such as fibroids (especially submucosal) and adenomyosis is assessed with transvaginal ultrasound, supporting an ultrasound-first uterine work-up.
Teratogenic/environmental exposures and periconceptual folate are relevant to pregnancy outcome counselling, supporting environmental risk assessment and preconception folate advice.
